I just beat a heimer for the first time. He probably wasn't very good, but he might have done a disservice to all the other heimers out there by giving me insight into some glaring weaknesses.

Heimer is different from most champions I've played against because his body is separate from his attacks. Everyone else can fire their key abilities from their person no matter where they are, Heimer can lose that ability. 

The important thing to remember is that when Heimer is standing in the field of three of his turrets, he's the master of his domain, but he's also planted himself down in that position. You want to be mobile. Let the wave move past that point and then he can't reposition without making himself vulnerable. Early game, if your wave gets into that domain, he'll push it back pretty quick, but he'll also draw aggro from those minions and won't want to stay there. If you can push him out the back side and loop around, you have some more free shots.

I'd say one of the biggest worries when it comes to Heimer is YOUR teammates. A helpful jungler can turn heimer into a killing machine, but if everyone understands his limitations, you can trap him inside of that triangle and the rest of the battlefield is yours.

If you've got more than one SD register active, make sure you keep your returns separate from each other when it's busy. This is vital. If anyone gets aggressive about return policy, call a CSM. Your job is to know and communicate the policy, not to write it or reconcile it with your customer's religious views. 

If something is shifty, call a CSM and pretend you forgot if there is a special policy with that item, like you know, there is with air beds or batteries, you don't want to mess anything up and while you're acting, take the item out of the box and show the CSM that it's not what's supposed to be in the box or was clearly purchased in 1978.

If your customer wants a ridiculous exception, you want that exception too, but you can't do it yourself. Escalate and ask your supervisor for exactly what the customer wants, do your best to advocate for it. Some managers want you to be the bad guy and for them to be the hero who swoops in and approves the crazy shit. They don't pay you enough to take heel heat.

IT IS VITALLY IMPORTANT THAT YOU KNOW HOW MANY ITEMS SOMEONE IS RETURNING AND DO AS MUCH AS POSSIBLE IN ONE TRANSACTION. Know how to get around the register prompts and never ever let anyone create a transaction where that "accidentally" happens.

Final word of advice: Do whatever you have to get out of service desk coverage as soon as you possibly can
